title: Guardrails and Failure Containment
html:
Chapter 8 established how Baodium measured customer-facing search latency. A few weeks later, customers began seeing slower search results, although the search application had not received a new deployment. Customers were waiting for search results and suggestions, so the engineers looked at other workloads sharing the search infrastructure.

The cause turned out to be a feature built by a different team. Catalog export let a merchant download every product listing as a spreadsheet. Because an export was, in effect, a long series of searches, it reused the search application’s client and worker pool. During the slowest periods, six exports were running concurrently. Each occupied a worker for several seconds and sent one cluster query per page of results, while as many as 40 customer searches waited in the pool’s queue. Query time inside the search cluster had also risen, from about 60 to 150 milliseconds, because the exports had multiplied the queries it received. Nothing stopped one export from consuming hundreds of times the backend time of a search, because the customer-facing workload had no allocation of its own.

If you have shared a home internet connection, you have lived through a version of this. Someone starts a large download, and your video call begins to freeze, although neither application is broken. Engineers call it the noisy neighbor problem, and it appears wherever different kinds of work share a resource. The team considered adding workers, but more workers would allow additional export queries into a cluster already under pressure. Shorter timeouts could interrupt individual exports without limiting the traffic from the others. The engineers needed one control over which work could occupy the application’s workers and another over how much of the cluster each workload could use. Later failures added a queue for long exports, a circuit breaker, rate limits, and a staged recovery procedure.

Interactive and Batch Workload Separation

The admission limit has to reflect how much of the shared resource each request uses. An interactive search returns one bounded page while a customer waits. An export retrieves many pages and writes them to a file that the merchant downloads later, as Table Table shows. Almost any interactive request and batch job differ in this way.

Because of that difference, a limit on incoming HTTP requests would treat a search and an export as equal, when in fact one export can send hundreds of cluster queries after its HTTP request has completed. The team split admission into two decisions. The first decides whether an export job may start, which limits how many exports run concurrently. The second decides whether a running job may send its next query, which limits how much of the cluster exports use. Checking each page separately also makes cancellation effective, because a canceled export stops before its next page instead of working through the rest of the catalog.

Exports also needed somewhere to run. The team first considered a single worker pool and letting customer searches jump to the front of its queue. That shortens the wait for searches already in the queue, but it does nothing about workers that exports have occupied for several seconds each, so a burst of exports can still fill the pool. Instead, exports got their own bounded executor. A separate executor sits partly idle when no exports are running, but it guarantees that exports never occupy the workers that serve customers, and the team judged that guarantee to be more valuable than the idle capacity. The export-job limit is checked before a job enters that executor’s queue. A job that waited for a permit inside the executor would take up a queue entry and memory while it waited, which would recreate the original queueing problem one level down.

Bulkheads and Resource Reservations

The separate executor solved the queueing problem but not the cluster problem, because export workers and search workers still query the same cluster. You met bulkheads in Chapter 4, where Order Service limited its outbound calls to Fraud Service. Here the same idea limits how much of a shared resource one workload can occupy. In the search application, every export query must acquire two permits, one from a small export allowance and one from the process’s pool of backend-call slots, as Figure Figure shows.

Suppose each process has eight backend-call slots and exports may use at most two of them. Exports can then never occupy more than two slots, and customer searches can use all eight whenever exports are idle. Think of a restaurant that seats large parties at no more than two of its eight tables, while walk-in customers may take any free table. The two-slot rule caps exports at two slots without reserving those slots for them. On a busy evening, a large party might wait a long time, because walk-ins can fill every table. The export allowance works the same way, so under sustained customer traffic, exports could wait indefinitely. If exports had to finish by a deadline, the team would need to reserve slots for them and accept that customer searches might be refused while reserved slots sat unused. Merchants could tolerate slower exports, but customers would not tolerate slower searches, which made the ceiling the right choice.

The ceiling works because each export releases its permit between pages, giving searches a chance to take the slot. Each export worker acquires a permit, retrieves one page, releases the permit, and only then writes the page to its output file. While the file is being written, the released slot can serve a customer search instead of sitting unused for several seconds. The cost is one permit acquisition per page, which is negligible next to the query itself. Buffering every page in memory and writing the file at the end would avoid even that cost, but a large catalog could exhaust the application’s memory, so each worker streams pages to bounded temporary storage instead.

Initial Concurrency Limits per Process

How many of the eight slots should exports get? The numbers eight and two began as estimates, so the team tested them. Because the decision was how many backend calls exports may use, the test changed only that number. Eight export jobs were queued throughout, the same customer searches, suggestions, and catalog sizes ran in every trial, and only the number of export permits changed between trials, with the results shown in Table Table.

With a search target of 300 milliseconds at the 95th percentile, two permits is the best of the three settings. Going from two to four adds only two completed exports per minute but pushes search latency to 680 milliseconds, because the extra export queries compete with searches inside the cluster. Before going to production, the two-permit setting also had to meet the search target with larger catalogs, uneven traffic across instances, and one instance unavailable. A limit chosen this way is much easier to defend than a rule of thumb, such as reserving a fixed percentage of the pool, because the team knows what the limit achieves and which measurement would justify changing it.

Limits Across the Fleet

Every number so far applies to one process, and that is easy to forget. Four processes each allow two export calls, so the cluster receives eight at most, or so it seems. A rolling deployment that briefly adds a fifth process raises the total to ten, and indexing jobs and administration tools query the cluster as well. This is the same arithmetic you used for database sessions in Chapter 2. The team worked down from the cluster’s tested capacity and recorded the reason for each step, as Table Table shows.

Laying the numbers out in this order shows which values depend on which measurements. If the deployment surge rose from five processes to six, for example, eight slots per process would use the entire allowance of 48 and leave no margin, so each process would drop to seven slots, two for exports and five for customer searches alone. The reservation of 16 queries for background callers depends just as much on those callers, because nothing in the search application can stop them from exceeding it. Baodium limits the indexing service to 12 concurrent queries and the administration tools to 4, each enforced by the caller, so that together they never exceed 16.

The application’s share can be divided among processes either as fixed shares or through a coordinated allocation. Fixed shares are simpler to operate but leave capacity unused when traffic is uneven across instances. A coordinated allocation uses capacity more fully, but it adds a dependency and needs a policy for when coordination fails, because a process that went on using an expired share could overlap with another process using the same capacity. Baodium chose fixed shares, since four instances rarely receive very uneven traffic, and a little unused capacity cost less than another dependency in the admission path.

Deferred Jobs and Queue Admission

The bulkhead protected customer searches, but it stretched large exports to several minutes, and an HTTP request open for that long was unreliable, because any network interruption lost the download. Merchants did not need an export to finish within one request, so the team changed submission to return a job reference as soon as the job was durably accepted. The merchant now checks progress and downloads the file when it is ready. In exchange, the team took on a job store, a status endpoint, and cleanup of finished files, a cost it accepted because each piece was simple and the download no longer depended on one long connection. This is the same asynchronous pattern Chapter 4 used for deferred fraud checks, and the one you see whenever a site emails you a link when your report or data export is ready.

The export queue needed a limit based on its promised completion time. At a tested rate of 20 exports per minute, 100 jobs already waiting could delay a new job by about five minutes, before any additional arrivals. Baodium tracked the oldest job’s age and admitted new exports only while the estimated delay was acceptable. Large catalogs used a separate class so a few slow exports could not occupy every worker.

An accepted job needs a durable identity, an owner, a status, and a recovery path in case its worker fails, and an application that cannot record those cannot truthfully report the job as accepted. When the backlog reaches its limit, a new submission receives a clear temporary refusal, and a repeated submission for an accepted job returns that job’s status instead of creating a copy. Chapter 12 examines durable delivery in detail. For guardrails, remember that accepting a job creates an obligation. The job must be finished, canceled, or marked as failed, so an accepted response must name an operation whose progress the merchant can check.

Decision review

Two slots or six?

Each search application process has eight backend-call slots, and exports may use at most two of them. A merchant complains that a catalog export now takes eleven minutes instead of four, and an engineer proposes raising the export allocation to six slots during off-peak hours, arguing that interactive traffic is low at 03:00 anyway.

Raise the export allocation to six during off-peak hours.

Leave the allocation at two and add more export workers.

Leave the allocation at two and give exports their own search replica.

A can work, but only with a safeguard decided in advance, because the off-peak assumption will sometimes be wrong. A promotion, customers in other time zones, or a retry storm from a daytime region can all bring interactive traffic into the window, and an allocation based on the clock has no way to notice. If you choose this option, tie the allocation to measured interactive demand rather than to the time of day, and reserve a floor of slots that exports can never take.

B does not increase export throughput, because the two backend permits are the limiting resource. Adding workers that compete for the same two permits completes the same amount of work, with more workers waiting.

C gives exports their own replica and query allocation, which removes direct competition for interactive query slots at the cost of another replica to operate and update. Shared indexing, storage, or network capacity can still connect the two workloads. This option fits when measured export demand cannot be met within the shared allocation without slowing interactive searches.

Circuit Breakers

A few weeks after these changes, an index rebuild left the search cluster slow for every caller for several minutes. The bulkhead offered no protection this time, because no single workload was crowding out the others. Everyone was suffering equally.

The search application went on sending queries to the overloaded cluster. Each query added to the overload, and each customer search spent its whole deadline waiting for a response that was likely to fail. Chapter 4 introduced the circuit breaker for this situation. It records the results of recent calls and, when too many fail or run slowly, stops sending calls for a while. That reduces the load on the dependency while it recovers and lets callers fail in milliseconds instead of waiting out their deadlines. Figure Figure shows the breaker’s three states and the conditions under which it changes state.

Closed.

Calls are permitted, and their results are recorded.

Open.

Calls are refused for a configured interval.

Half-open.

A limited number of probe calls test whether normal admission can resume.

For search, the breaker treats transport failures, timeouts, and responses slower than the caller’s allocated time as bad results. An empty result is a valid response, not a dependency failure, so it is recorded as a success. While the breaker is open, export workers reschedule their next query according to the job policy instead of polling the breaker, and customer searches receive the supported unavailable response or the fallback described later in the chapter.

Choosing Thresholds

A breaker that opens too readily turns ordinary noise into an outage, and one that opens too slowly provides no protection, so each threshold has to be set against the cluster’s normal behavior. In this example, an interactive search call may take at most 400 milliseconds, or less if the caller’s deadline is shorter. After reviewing representative successful calls, the engineers chose 250 milliseconds as the slow-call threshold. Listing Listing shows the resulting policy for one process.

You rarely need to write a breaker yourself. Libraries such as Resilience4j for Java, Polly for .NET, and gobreaker for Go provide one, and most expose settings very close to these, such as a sliding window, a minimum number of calls, failure and slow-call rate thresholds, and an open interval. The thresholds depend on each service’s latency targets, resource limits, and observed failure rate.

The window had to contain enough calls to mean something. Without a minimum number of calls, a handful of failures during a quiet minute would produce a large percentage and open the breaker for no reason. The thresholds were then set far above normal behavior. Failures were normally rare, so a threshold of half of all calls could be reached only by a problem affecting most of the cluster, and the slow-call threshold sat many times above the share of slow calls on an ordinary day. Export page retrieval normally takes longer than a search, so exports need their own latency threshold. Combining the two workloads under one threshold could open the breaker during ordinary export activity.

The 10-second open interval came from earlier incidents, in which cluster overload had lasted between 5 and 30 seconds, and a small random variation across processes stops their probes from arriving together. Because the rebuild lasted far longer than those episodes, the breaker cycled repeatedly through opening, probing, and reopening, and that cycling spared the cluster most of the load until the rebuild finished. A longer interval would suit an outage of that length, but it would leave search unavailable longer than necessary during the far more frequent short episodes, so the team retained 10 seconds. The breaker also reacts before its full window has elapsed. Once the minimum sample exists, it evaluates its thresholds as each result arrives. Calls that have not yet completed contribute no result, however, so in the first seconds of a slowdown, before the breaker has evidence, the concurrency limits are the only protection the cluster has.

Half-Open Probes and Recovery

A half-open probe should exercise the operation that failed, so the search probe is an ordinary bounded query rather than a request to a health endpoint that shows only that the process responds. Even so, three successful probes are weak evidence of full recovery, because three calls say nothing about how the cluster performs under full load. The breaker closes into the same concurrency limits as before, and the team resumes export processing in stages, checking search latency and export completion between increases, because queued exports and delayed retries released together could recreate the overload. Electricity grids restore power after a blackout the same way, one district at a time, because switching every district back on together would overload the grid again.

Probes also multiply across the fleet, and restarting a process resets most local breaker implementations. A fleet that restarts repeatedly during an outage sends repeated waves of calls to a failing dependency, which is one more reason the liveness checks from Chapter 6 should not depend on a shared dependency. The recovery tests at the end of the chapter include this case.

Rate Limits and Retry Budgets

While investigating the rebuild, the team looked at where the cluster’s load was coming from, and two findings led to the next controls. Both involve rate limits, which are easy to confuse with the concurrency limits used so far. Think of a stadium entrance. The number of people allowed inside the building is a concurrency limit, and the number allowed through the turnstiles each minute is a rate limit. A concurrency limit controls how much processing is outstanding, whereas a rate limit controls how often new attempts begin. Neither replaces the other, because a few slots can issue many requests per second to a fast cluster, while a permitted request rate can use up those slots once responses slow down.

Burst Allowance

Rate limits are usually implemented as a token bucket. Each attempt uses up a token, and tokens are added back at a configured rate, up to a maximum balance. A bucket refilling at 100 tokens per second with a burst allowance of 10 can briefly admit more than 100 requests in a second. The burst allowance should match what the dependency can serve without exceeding its queue or latency limits.

For a single service instance, the token bucket in Listing Listing uses a monotonic clock and a lock, so concurrent request handlers cannot both spend the same token. The example in Listing Listing is deliberately local to one process.

import time
from threading import Lock

class TokenBucket:
    def __init__(self, rate, burst):
        self.rate, self.burst = rate, burst
        self.tokens, self.updated = burst, time.monotonic()
        self.lock = Lock()

    def allow(self):
        with self.lock:
            now = time.monotonic()
            self.tokens = min(self.burst, self.tokens +
                              (now - self.updated) * self.rate)
            self.updated = now
            if self.tokens < 1:
                return False
            self.tokens -= 1
            return True

With rate=100 and burst=10, this bucket admits an initial burst of ten attempts and replenishes tokens at 100 per second. The refill rate and burst allowance need testing against the provider’s actual limit. Because each instance has its own bucket, ten instances would create ten independent allowances. For a fleet-wide limit, we could use a shared Redis bucket with an atomic Lua script or a gateway such as Envoy with a global rate-limit service. A shared limiter also requires a policy for what happens when the limiter itself is unavailable.1 When a request exceeds its allowed rate, an HTTP API can respond with 429 Too Many Requests. A Retry-After header can indicate when the client may attempt another request, provided the service can estimate that interval reliably. If you have used a public API such as GitHub’s, you have probably received one.

Choosing the Rate-Limit Key

The first finding concerned a merchant integration. Besides the storefront and exports, the search application serves a merchant search API that merchants’ own systems call, and one large merchant was polling its listings through eight API keys at a combined 400 requests per second, roughly a quarter of the cluster’s query load. Limiting that traffic raises the central design decision in rate limiting. Whose bucket should each request draw from? That choice decides whether one caller can use up an allowance meant for everyone. Each of the four candidate keys produces a different outcome for this merchant.

Per IP address.

Many customers share carrier and corporate addresses, and an integration can rotate addresses, so this key measures network location rather than the caller.

Per API key.

At 50 requests per second per key, the merchant’s eight keys admitted all 400 requests, and every additional key raises the allowance by another 50.

Per merchant.

The server resolves each key to its merchant and charges the merchant’s bucket. At 20 requests per second with a burst of 40, the integration received 20 requests per second, and other merchants retained their share.

Fleet-wide per operation class.

This key protects the cluster’s total allowance, but on its own it lets the largest caller take most of that allowance.

Baodium uses two keys together, and a request must pass both. The per-merchant bucket provides fairness among merchants, and the fleet-wide bucket protects the cluster, because many merchants who are each within their quota can together exceed what the cluster can serve. Any multi-tenant API faces the same choice, and the usual design is the same pair of keys, one per tenant for fairness and one global key for protection. Retries are charged to the same merchant bucket as first attempts, so a client that retries aggressively spends its own allowance rather than its neighbors’. The merchant identity comes from the authenticated key on the server, never from a field the client supplies, because a client could otherwise claim to be another merchant. Exports use the same pattern, with a per-merchant quota on accepted jobs and a backend limit that includes calls from every merchant.

Retries as Additional Load

The second finding was that retries had increased the load on the cluster during the rebuild. The search client retried every timed-out call once, so when 20 percent of 100 first attempts per second timed out, the cluster received 120 attempts per second, a 20 percent increase at the moment it had the least spare capacity.

A retry budget, which Chapter 4 mentioned briefly, limits retries to a fraction of recent first attempts. At 5 percent, it permits about five retries per second at that rate, and the other candidates receive the configured failure response. The trade-off is deliberate. Some requests that a retry would have rescued now fail, but the cluster is spared extra load at the point where that load does the most damage. The budget also needs a maximum balance and an accounting interval, because credit saved during hours of healthy traffic could otherwise fund a large burst of retries during an outage. You may not need to build this yourself either. gRPC, for example, has a built-in retry throttling setting that works in this way, disabling retries when too many recent calls have failed.

Backoff and jitter spread retries over time but do not limit how many happen, so they complement a retry budget rather than replace it. Each retry must also fit within the caller’s deadline and pass the breaker, rate, and concurrency checks. As Chapter 4 showed, retries at several layers multiply, so the team made the search client the only layer allowed to retry and confirmed that the gateway and SDK added no retries of their own. No backend-call slot is assigned during backoff, and an export worker returns its job to a scheduled state rather than occupying a worker while it waits.

Fallbacks and Load Shedding

With the cluster protected, the team turned to a decision every product manager eventually faces. What should a customer see when search cannot be served?

One proposal was to query the primary product database whenever search was unavailable. A fallback helps only if the application can produce it during the failure it is meant to handle, and this one would send every refused search to a database that had never been tested with that workload, spreading the failure to a second system. Most fallbacks draw on some other resource in this way, so ask of any fallback which resource it uses and whether that resource has capacity to spare during the same failure. The team chose a narrower fallback, returning a recent cached result for popular queries and a clear temporary-unavailable response for everything else. Unrelated results would mislead the customer, and so would an empty list, which implies that no matching products exist.

Load shedding means dropping, refusing, or deferring work that the application is allowed to leave out when demand exceeds capacity. The term comes from electricity grids, which cut power to some areas on purpose during extreme demand so that the whole grid does not fail. The work to shed is the work that uses the constrained resource. If the cluster is the bottleneck, pausing export queries helps, but disabling an analytics task that never queries the cluster frees no search capacity. For the same reason, a shedding order is defined per resource and enforced where that resource is admitted. CPU scheduling priority cannot do this job, because a low-priority thread that has acquired a search slot occupies the slot until it finishes.

Suggestions complicated the earlier arithmetic, because they query the cluster too. If suggestions could take shared slots freely, two exports and three suggestions could leave only three of the eight slots for customer searches. The team turned the export permit into an optional-work permit that exports and suggestions share, so that together they never occupy more than two slots. Before adopting it, the team reran the concurrency test with both workloads drawing on the same two permits. Search latency met its target, fewer than 1 percent of suggestion requests were left out at peak, and export throughput fell from about 21 to about 18 jobs per minute, which the export completion target could tolerate. Listing Listing shows the resulting admission configuration for each process.

Optional work can occupy at most two of the eight slots, which leaves at least six that it never uses, while customer searches may take any slot that is free. Customer searches are never refused to make room for optional work, although they can be refused when all eight slots are busy and their 250-millisecond queue is full. Within the optional allowance, exports give way first. An export is admitted only while fewer than five shared slots are busy, whereas a suggestion is admitted while fewer than six are busy, because a customer is waiting for the suggestion and an export can resume later. These occupancy checks are not atomic, so concurrent requests can pass them using the same reading, but the semaphores still limit optional work to two concurrent calls, so such a race cannot reduce the capacity protected for customer searches. Chapter 14 applies the same structure to payment-provider capacity, where captures, refunds, and reconciliation each receive a reserved share of calls.

Table Table lists other reduced responses and the database or provider operations each one avoids. Two rules apply to all of them. Deferred work lengthens the backlog if producers go on sending at the same rate, so every queue needs a limit, and financial records and required audit events can never inherit the omission policy of optional analytics. Priority must also be assigned by a trusted rule on the server. If callers could mark their own work as urgent, every caller would, and the reservation would protect nothing.

Token-Bucket and Concurrency Enforcement

Every policy in this chapter depends on admission checks that reserve capacity atomically. As Chapters 1 and 4 explained, reading an in-flight gauge and then deciding is not enough, because several requests can read the same free slot and all proceed. This mistake is known as check-then-act, and a semaphore prevents it by letting only one request acquire the last permit.

An export query needs two permits, an optional-work permit and a shared backend permit, and Listing Listing acquires them without blocking. If the shared permit is unavailable, the optional-work permit is released and the request takes its refusal or deferral path. The client and deadline interfaces in the listing are illustrative.

from threading import BoundedSemaphore

optional_slots = BoundedSemaphore(2)   # exports and suggestions
backend_slots = BoundedSemaphore(8)

def fetch_export_page(query, deadline):
    if not optional_slots.acquire(blocking=False):
        raise ExportCapacityUnavailable()

    try:
        if not backend_slots.acquire(blocking=False):
            raise SearchCapacityUnavailable()

        try:
            deadline.require_time_for_attempt()

            return search_client.fetch_page(
                query=query,
                deadline=deadline,
            )
        finally:
            backend_slots.release()
    finally:
        optional_slots.release()

Suggestions acquire the same two permits through their own function, and customer searches acquire only the shared backend permit. Because each process has its own semaphore objects, these numbers are local limits, and the fleet total depends on the allocation in Table Table. The client call must also finish its local work before the function returns, because a call that returned a future while execution continued would release its permits too early.

A local permit also cannot confirm that the remote query has stopped, for the reasons Chapter 4 described. If the client gives up at its deadline while the cluster is still running the query, releasing the permit lets a new query start alongside the old one, and a process can then have more than eight queries running in the cluster. The fleet allocation works only if the cluster enforces its own query timeout close to the client’s deadline. Check this for your own search engine rather than assuming it. Many engines, Elasticsearch among them, treat a per-request timeout as best effort, returning partial results while some of the work may continue. Baodium verified that canceling a query on the client stopped it on the cluster.

The breaker and rate limiter also have to be combined with the semaphores carefully. If a half-open probe receives permission from the breaker but cannot acquire a backend slot, the implementation must return that permission without recording a failed call. Mistakes in cancellation and partial admission like these can leak permits slowly or admit more work than the configuration allows, so each one needs its own test.

Admission for State-Changing Operations

Rejecting a search before execution changes no business state. Payment and inventory operations need more care. An admission refusal before dispatch means no new attempt started, while a timeout after dispatch leaves the remote outcome unresolved. The handler checks the durable operation record before returning a final status, and recovery uses the original operation identifier from Chapter 3. Status queries and reconciliation need reserved capacity even when new writes are refused.

Calibration and Recovery Testing

By the recovery rehearsal, search had per-workload admission limits, a circuit breaker, and a retry budget. The engineers tested them together because queued exports and delayed retries could compete with customer searches as the cluster recovered.

A natural alternative is to make the limits adapt automatically to measured latency. Adaptive limits exist and are useful. Netflix’s open-source concurrency-limits library and Envoy’s adaptive concurrency filter both adjust limits from observed latency, borrowing ideas from the way the Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) adjusts its sending rate to network congestion. They make sense when available capacity varies widely. A controller that reacts to every latency sample tends to oscillate, raising and lowering admission repeatedly, and a stable one needs measurement windows, bounded adjustments, separate conditions for lowering and restoring limits, and a policy for stale data. Because the search cluster’s capacity was stable, fixed and tested limits, along with a way to pause exports, gave the team the containment it needed without that complexity.

The SLO indicators from Chapter 8 show the customer consequences of these limits, but they should not drive admission on their own, because rejected requests are bad events in the SLO. A rule that rejected more requests whenever the burn rate rose would reinforce the condition that triggered it.

Failure-Containment Test Plan

The test begins with representative customer searches, suggestions, and a realistic mix of catalog sizes for exports, sent by a load generator that maintains a fixed arrival rate, as Chapter 1 recommended.

Exports are then added until the application reaches its configured limits, and the engineers confirm that accepted work is bounded, that refusals are recorded, and that customer searches retain their six protected slots while exports and suggestions are both at their limits. Next, cluster responses are delayed and selected calls are prevented from completing, which exercises the seconds before the breaker opens. The cluster is then restored while queued jobs and retry candidates are waiting, and the test continues until the backlog clears. If the first probes succeed and the cluster then overloads again, the staged recovery policy needs revision. Finally, the engineers repeat the relevant cases with one instance unavailable and during a deployment, because both conditions change how local limits add up across the fleet.

The test report shows accepted, completed, refused, and timed-out work, together with queue age and customer-facing latency, because latency for completed requests alone can improve just because the application refused most of them. Each refusal is recorded with the active policy version and its reason. When refusals rise, an engineer can then tell whether they came from the merchant quota, the optional-work allowance, the shared backend limit, or an open breaker.

Field note

Amazon S3, February 2017

On February 28, 2017, an authorized Amazon S3 engineer was investigating slow responses in the S3 billing system in the US-EAST-1 region. An incorrect input to a command intended to remove a small number of servers removed far more than intended, including servers supporting the index and placement subsystems, on which every S3 request in the region depended. Both subsystems had to be fully restarted, and because they had become substantially larger since their last full restart, recovery took much longer than expected.

AWS changed the tool to remove capacity more slowly and to refuse any removal that would take a subsystem below its minimum required capacity. These admission checks limit the damage a mistake can do, because no process prevents every mistake. They are guardrails in the sense used at the start of this chapter. The long restart teaches a separate lesson, which is that a recovery procedure has to be tested at the scale at which it will be needed in production.

Source: published incident report.

Per-Tenant and Fleet-Wide Provider Limits

These controls carry over when the shared resource belongs to someone else. Imagine a SaaS product that sends customer documents to a third-party analysis API. The provider allows 1,000 requests per second for your whole organization. One tenant starts a large import and asks for 800 analyses a second, while everyone else together asks for 500. Forwarding all 1,300 only hands the overload to the provider, and if your client retries every rejection, the provider receives even more.

Two limits solve the fairness and the safety problem together. A fleet-wide limit caps the organization at the provider’s contract, and a per-tenant allocation stops one customer from taking the whole of it. Both are checked before a request leaves. A token bucket controls the rate, and a separate semaphore controls how many calls are in flight, because a slow provider can tie up your workers and connections long before you reach its per-second limit. Chapter 4 covers the deadlines and retry ownership those calls also need.

The fleet-wide limit has to be shared across instances. If each of ten instances runs its own local bucket sized at 900 calls a second, the effective ceiling becomes ten times what you intended. Reserving part of the allowance for critical work, say 100 calls a second for operations that must not wait, is a policy choice, and the class allocations together must still fit inside the provider’s budget.

A circuit breaker addresses a different question, whether the provider is healthy. A tenant hitting its own quota says nothing about the provider’s health, so quota rejections must never open the breaker. Rejected requests need a clear response that tells the caller whether and when to retry, and work deferred into a queue needs a bounded backlog, an expiry rule, and a worker rate fast enough to clear it while normal traffic continues.

The design review ends with a slowdown test. If each provider call starts taking six times longer, the number of calls in flight rises sixfold at the same request rate, and the concurrency limit begins turning requests away well before the per-second limit is reached. That is the protection working as intended, provided the application has already decided what the turned-away requests become. Short Message Service (SMS) gateways, payment providers, cloud APIs, and hosted models all call for the same four controls, one each for rate, concurrency, retries, and priority.

Summary

The export incident shows how a neighbor sharing its resources can slow a healthy service that has no bug at all. Whenever different kinds of work share workers, a connection pool, or a cluster, the heaviest kind will take as much as it is allowed to take. Guardrails decide in advance how much that is.

The tools in this chapter each address a different question, and they are easier to use when you treat them separately. Workload separation and bulkheads decide which work may occupy which resources. Queues decide what waits and for how long. Circuit breakers stop calls that are likely to fail. Rate limits and retry budgets cap how much any caller, including your own retry logic, may send. Load shedding decides what to drop when everything else is full. Each limit is a measured number, and the recovery test matters as much as the outage test, because releasing a backlog in one burst can recreate the overload you just escaped.

Those measured numbers describe the code that was running when they were measured. A release that makes each query more expensive can invalidate them, and Chapter 10 begins with that kind of release.

Hidden assumptions

Assumption and scope & Interactive search, suggestions, and merchant exports can share execution resources because they use the same backend API.
Condition that tests it & Export demand or slow cluster responses use up the shared execution slots.
Constraint or invariant & Export jobs, export queries, and the job backlog have separate limits. Exports and suggestions share a two-slot optional allowance inside the eight shared slots, every process adds to fleet usage, and background callers enforce a combined reservation of 16.
Evidence and uncertainty & Concurrency tests that vary only backend permits, with suggestions active, compare search latency with export throughput.

Still unknown: how catalog size, uneven traffic, deployment overlap, and queries that continue after client cancellation change resource usage.
Signal and evaluation window & Interactive latency, permit use, rejected work, and breaker samples, measured over each overload test.
Control and decision & Limit export jobs before they are queued, protect customer searches from optional work, refuse new jobs when the backlog cannot meet the promised completion time, and resume deferred work in stages after recovery.
Owner and review trigger & The search team owns backend-call policy, the merchant-feature owner defines export acceptance and completion commitments, and the platform team verifies shared capacity and deployment accounting. Review after an overload or dependency failure, and before expanding exports to more merchants.
